concept.name: Bull put spread
concept.definition: A bull put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short put at a higher strike and a long put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays above the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (credit) and maximum loss.
concept.intuition: You sell a put betting the stock stays up, and buy a cheaper lower put as insurance so a sell-off can't cost more than a known amount.
concept.mechanics: Net credit at entry; maximum gain = credit at or above the short strike; maximum loss = (strike width - credit) at or below the long strike. It is the credit-spread counterpart of the bull call spread, with nearly identical payoff at equivalent strikes.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K2 - K1) - net credit; breakeven = K2 - net credit, where K1 < K2 are the put strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Gap-down moves can blow through both strikes and realize maximum loss with no chance to adjust; short-leg assignment before ex-dividend or at expiration can leave unwanted long stock.
concept.misconceptions: Choosing far-OTM strikes for a '90% win rate' does not create an edge: the credit shrinks toward the risk-free compensation for the residual tail risk, and one max-loss wipes out many wins.
concept.example: Sell the XYZ $100 put for $3, buy the $95 put for $1: credit $2. If XYZ stays at or above $100, keep $200; at or below $95, lose $300.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
